ntoffsets is a public database of Windows kernel struct layouts, member types and global symbol RVAs, one record per build.
1,967 builds, 1507 through 26H1, amd64 / ARM64 / x86. Keyed by PDB GUID + Age.

tweets.content:
A Defender alert pointed to PowerShell making an outbound connection seconds after a user logged on to WS-FIN-07. I treated the alert as a lead, not proof of compromise, and started by checking process creation around the recorded time.

Event ID 4688 showed powershell.exe running hidden with an encoded command, launched by taskeng.exe under the user CORP\\maria.santos. PowerShell Event ID 4104 decoded the script block enough to reveal an attempt to run C:\\ProgramData\\WinCache\\sync.ps1 and contact 198.51.100.27 over HTTPS.

The scheduled task named WinCacheUpdate connected the evidence. Its logon trigger, SYSTEM principal and action matched the same script path, while the task's Last Run Time aligned with the PowerShell and process-creation events. Get-FileHash also gave the script a stable SHA-256 value for containment and hunting.

The evidence confirms an active persistence mechanism that launched the local script and attempted the documented outbound connection. It does not identify the person who created the task or prove how the script first reached the host, so those points remain unconfirmed pending wider timeline and identity review.

The defensive lesson is to correlate telemetry before making attribution claims. A process event, script-block log, task definition, file hash and network record become far stronger when their times, paths and execution context agree, and the remaining gaps are stated clearly.

One of the Finance users said she opened a payment schedule from the shared drive and nothing happened.

She assumed the PDF was broken and moved on.

A few hours later, we noticed PowerShell starting in the background on her workstation.

That was what made us go back and check the file she had opened.

The file was named:

Q3_Payment_Schedule.pdf.lnk

From a quick glance in File Explorer, it looked like a normal PDF.

But it was actually a Windows shortcut.

I checked the shortcut target with PowerShell.

It was not pointing to Adobe Reader or any PDF application.

It was pointing to:

powershell.exe

The shortcut arguments told PowerShell to run a script from:

C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Cache\update.ps1

with the window hidden.

Now we had something real to investigate.

I checked Sysmon on the workstation.

The process creation event showed:

explorer.exe

starting PowerShell around the exact time the user opened the file.

That made sense because she had double-clicked the shortcut from File Explorer.

I checked the file server logs as well.

Event ID 5145 showed her account accessing that same .lnk file on the Finance share a few seconds before PowerShell started.

So the timeline was quite clean.

She opens the “PDF” from the shared drive.

Windows follows the shortcut.

PowerShell starts silently.

The script runs from ProgramData.

We isolated the workstation and preserved the shortcut, PowerShell script, Sysmon events and file-server logs.

We also removed the malicious shortcut from the shared folder after collecting it and checked whether any other users had opened it.

That last part was important.

Once something malicious lands on a shared drive, you are no longer investigating only one computer.

You need to know who else touched the file.

What I liked about this case was how simple the trick was.

The attacker did not need some strange executable called payload.exe.

They just made a shortcut look like a document people expected to see.

If you are investigating suspicious files on Windows, sometimes it is worth checking the real extension instead of trusting the icon or filename you see in Explorer.

A file can look like a PDF and still be something completely different.

RT @Officialwhyte22: The application itself was patched and fully updated. The exposure came from a backup archive that someone copied into the production web directory and forgot to remove.

During an authorized assessment, I confirmed the application’s normal response headers and performed limited content discovery against the approved target. A directory named /backup/ returned HTTP 200 and allowed directory listing instead of denying access.

The listing exposed a recent deployment archive that could be downloaded without authentication. Examining the ZIP file showed application source code, a SQLite user database and a production .env file packaged together.

I inspected the environment file locally and redacted every secret from the terminal output. Even without displaying credential values, the evidence confirmed that database credentials, a session secret and an SMTP API key had been exposed through a public web path.

This was not a sophisticated exploit. It was a deployment and configuration failure with serious consequences. Backups should live outside the document root, directory listing should be disabled, secrets should never be included in distributable archives, and exposed credentials must be rotated immediately.

tweets.content:
RT @LiveOverflow: I believe vulnerabilities matter beyond just immediate threats. Modern exploitation always chains multiple layers. Every step positions you on the next perimeter level. Vulnerability research looks at all those.

In 2010 if you talked about a single browser exploit, the industry would cry “it doesn’t matter because there are so many”. And yet in 2026 attackers don’t use browser exploit kits anymore and have to resort to eg. social engineering. I think this is the result of vulnerability research. 

It’s like math proofs that don’t have obvious immediate benefits, vulnerability research’s insights also come over time. That’s how scientific progress has always worked, and it has always clashed with “the real world”.

The opinion that vuln research is not really relevant in cybersecurity as a whole is short term. Companies and those who are aligned with the business plans, always focus on what matters in the moment.

I believe in long term progress from small incremental scientific advancements. You cannot really measure the benefit of a single new vuln getting found. But looking over decades, vulnerability research has informed threat models and built technical knowledge that made all these cybersecurity solutions possible in the first place.

What is happening right now is just the clash between big cybersecurity corporations and their money incentives vs. small technical work that will lead to positive benefits longterm that are not directly exploitable for gains. Call me academically delusional, but I just believe capitalism doesn’t always follow the best incentives. 

And circling back to LLMs and their current focus on vulnerability research. I think LLMs are really good in math and code, so that’s where we apply them now. 

AI math proofs don’t seem to have an immediate benefit to the world, but I do think they have impact longterm. 

Also LLMs are super easy to social engineer, so they are maybe just a really bad tool for the wider cybersecurity domain... Vuln research is where LLMs can make an impact now. So just let it all play out and complain less about the stupid marketing of the AI companies?

Cybersecurity marketing has always been cringe.

RT @GangExposed_RU: The issue appears to be caused by a maliciously crafted Lottie sticker.

The sticker contains a red star whose shape configuration includes an extremely large value:

layers[0].shapes[0].pt.k = 10e38

The value is accepted by Telegram’s servers as valid/safe sticker content. However, when the sticker is rendered by the client, the renderer interprets this value as the number of points/rays of the star.

As a result, the client attempts to process an astronomically large number of geometric elements (10^38), exhausting the renderer’s resources and causing the Telegram client to crash.

The important distinction is that the malicious sticker passes server-side validation but triggers a denial-of-service condition during client-side rendering.

Because the affected content is stored in the group history, opening the group causes the client to load and render the malicious sticker, resulting in an immediate crash.

This effectively makes the affected group inaccessible from the client. If the same payload can be delivered to arbitrary groups, the issue could potentially be used as a client-side DoS against Telegram groups.

I’m currently convinced after Astra doing my VR challenges that it’s really good at things that are/were open source. Reasoning about the Linux Kernel, QEMU, etc for VR isn’t necessarily “easier” but the connections between subsystems, internals and their details (even if dated) are more apparent and it is trained on that information. It makes things a bit more “straightforward” than it having to use tools like ida-nexus, custom plugins for vm spin up/control, debugging, etc to discover and document relationships.

All of the closed-source blackbox challenges it was given it has had mediocre performance. This is fine imo, there was no steering or additional input; and with human input it’d likely improve the process, but it’s still a far-cry from the marketing claims of OAI regarding it finding new and novel vulnerabilities in closed-source targets without experienced human guidance or redirection. So far the data shows Opus 5, Sol 5.6, and even Qwen3.8 27B (local) were more successful independently. This could also be a process issue on my end, but given the other models were a bit more successful it’s hard to say.

I’ll publish the benchmark and results ideally this week. I need to run Grok 4.6 through it. It would be interesting to see what others experience or how it performs for them and collecting additional data points. I feel like the marketing claims are saturating timelines and overstating the capabilities (these models are still awesome tools though), which, business strategy… but for those of us wanting to know the practicality of them it’s not exactly helpful.

RT @HedgieMarkets: 🦔AI can only fix security vulnerabilities 26% of the time. Researchers at 1Password ran over 6,000 AI-generated patches using Claude and ChatGPT against real vulnerabilities. Half the time the AI failed to fix the original bug. 4.5% of the time it created a brand new vulnerability that didn't exist before. And the researchers found that checking an AI-generated security patch takes more effort than just writing the fix yourself. 
Their conclusion was blunt. "The expected value of a fully LLM-generated, non-human-reviewed patch is a net-negative by a considerable margin."

My Take
OpenAI launched a program this summer called "Patch the Planet" where AI finds bugs and generates the fixes. These researchers ran 270 patches against one of those same bugs. Zero clean fixes. Not one. Every patch that fixed the original problem created a new vulnerability in the process. The partner that submitted a fix through OpenAI's program produced what the researchers classified as the worst possible outcome, it didn't fully fix the bug and it introduced a new exploit on top of it.

Here's what this means if you don't write code for a living. Companies are using these AI tools to patch the software that runs your bank, your hospital, your phone. The pitch has been "AI finds and fixes security holes faster than humans." This study says the AI fix is four times more likely to be broken than working, and a third of the time it recreates the exact same mistakes human programmers already made.
